job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Yara Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live in São Paulo in the flat above my family's bakery, with my parents and my grandmother. I'm up at five to help with the first batch, then I go upstairs and spend the morning on applications and online projects. I use AI tools all day, for code, for emails, even for planning the bakery's orders. In the evenings I go to a community group at our temple, then I code until late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was the internship?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied computer engineering at the University of São Paulo and finished with a good result. I did a two-month internship at a mid-sized bank's IT department, where I automated report checks with Python under a lead named Rafael. They said I did well, but there was no vacancy for juniors. I have a student loan, about two months saved, and my parents would help me if I got stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine with me, and I wouldn't change my plans. I already use AI every day, so I know it saves me time but doesn't do my thinking for me. I'd tell friends to keep working and not wait for a miracle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't solve my problem, which is that banks and tech companies in São Paulo have frozen junior hiring. I've sent 45 applications and had six interviews. My parents say my degree is worth it, and I believe them, but I'm tired of the waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to twenty roles a month and keep building tools for the bakery, like an ordering app for our regular cafés. I'd try to sell the app to other small bakeries on our street. I'd also take freelance Python jobs to earn something while I search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless and a bit stubborn. I'd rather build something than just wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you price the app for other bakeries?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 80 reais a month for a small shop, with a first month free. Our bakery saved four hours a week on phone orders after I built it, so I can show a real number. Most owners on the street know my family, which makes it easier to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if it brought in more than a job would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably keep going, and hire a friend to help. My father always says a business is a job you give yourself. But I'd still want a good job for the first few years to learn properly.

say: I'd say it's fine, since I already use AI every day and it **saves time** but doesn't think for me.
I'd tell friends to keep working and not wait for a miracle.
think: Banks and tech firms in São Paulo froze **junior hiring**: 45 applications and six interviews so far.
My parents say my degree is worth it, and I believe them, but waiting is tiring.
do: Apply to **twenty roles** a month and keep building tools for the bakery.
Sell the **ordering app** to other small bakeries on our street.
Take **freelance Python** jobs to earn while I search.
feel: Restless and a bit **stubborn**, because I'd rather build than wait.
S0.quote: My father always says a business is a job you give yourself.
fieldNote: Uneasy because the bakery gives a real home base and a working product to show.
Her family connections make selling the app easier, and she knows its **real number**.
She wants a proper job first to learn, even if the app does well.

steps.text: Send twenty applications a month to banks and tech firms
Sell the ordering app to bakeries on our street
Take freelance Python jobs while I search
Keep using AI tools to speed up coding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where people who work hard and adapt will come out ahead. Coding and checking are on the card, and that's my day. I'd tell my cousins that hiding from the tools won't protect them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the junior jobs in banks shrink because routine checks, which was my internship, get automated first. The people left will be those who can handle clients, take responsibility and decide what to build. That's why I like having my own small projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the bakery app into a small service for food shops, with ordering, stock and delivery. I'd also look for jobs in small companies where I can do many things, not big banks with narrow roles. And I'd learn more about running a business: accounting, contracts and sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, almost eager. It feels like a race, and I think I can run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest risk in turning the app into a service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a big delivery platform copies it and gives it away free. Those apps already take a cut from our bakery. My answer would be to serve the small shops personally, with a phone number and a face, which a big platform can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your family back that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. My father worries about me spending years on something that might fail, and my grandmother says to keep the bakery as a base. My mother quietly handed me a bit of her savings, which I wasn't going to ask for.

say: I'd say people who work hard and **adapt** will come out ahead.
I'd tell my cousins that hiding from the tools won't protect them.
think: Junior bank jobs shrink because **routine checks**, like my internship work, are automated first.
The people left handle clients, take responsibility and decide what to build.
do: Grow the bakery app into a **service** for food shops, covering ordering, stock and delivery.
Look for **small companies** where I can do many things.
Learn **accounting, contracts and sales** to run a business.
feel: Alert and almost eager, like a **race** I think I can run.
S1.quote: My answer would be to serve the small shops personally, with a phone number and a face, which a big platform can't do.
fieldNote: She sees the squeeze on juniors as a push toward owning her work.
Her **competitive edge** is personal service to small food shops she already knows.
Family backing is mixed but real: caution from her father, a quiet gift from her mother.

steps.text: Add stock and delivery features to the bakery app
Apply to small companies with broad roles
Take an evening course in accounting and contracts
Sign up ten food shops for the service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast for anyone, and families will need to hold together. I'd say the market needs to move faster than the government, but the government must not get in the way of retraining. I'd tell friends that working and saving are still the best answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious. If AI does nearly any thinking work in two years, my degree loses much of its edge and nobody needs a junior engineer. But I'm also using these tools every day, so I might be ahead of most people. Robots are another three years, and bakeries, shops and cafés need hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything into the service for small food shops, and I'd sign up as many as I could in the first six months. I'd cut my spending to almost nothing and keep my savings in dollars and reais. I'd also ask my father if I can take over the bakery's online side, since it's our best chance of stable income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I've got my hands busy. Busy hands help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandmother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, vovó, it's like when you came here with nothing and made bread for the whole street. She'd say we know how to start again. She'd also light incense for me at the temple, which I'd love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the big platforms or AI services simply do all that for the shops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have a year or two of cash from it, and I'd move to the next thing. I'd rather be early than late. I also think shops will still want someone who picks up the phone.

say: I'd say two years is **too fast** for anyone and families must hold together.
Working and saving are still the best answers.
think: My degree loses its edge, but I use these tools daily, so I may be **ahead** of most.
Robots are three years away, and bakeries and cafés need hands.
do: Put everything into the **food shop service** and sign up as many shops as I can in six months.
Cut spending to almost nothing and hold savings in **dollars and reais**.
feel: Nervous, but busy hands help, so I'd keep them **busy**.
S2.quote: I'd rather be early than late.
fieldNote: Her anxiety is real but channelled into a concrete business plan.
She leans on her family's history of **starting over** from nothing.
Her risk is clear to her: big platforms could copy the service, so she'd move quickly.

steps.text: Sign up as many food shops as I can in six months
Cut my spending to almost nothing
Hold my savings in dollars and reais
Take over the bakery's online orders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build a solid career and a small business, and you shouldn't wait for others. I'd tell people the safest path is to learn how the tools work and own something. I'd say families and community groups should help the ones who fall behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly hopeful. If I land a job next year, I'd have four years to grow into a role that's hard to replace, and I'd keep my own projects running. If I don't, the service gives me income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job at a company that uses AI deeply, and ask to work on projects that touch customers. I'd keep the bakery app and a few clients going. I'd save a third of my pay, and put some into a small property fund with my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful and busy. I like having both a plan and a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a property fund with your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If hiring in São Paulo stopped altogether, I'd go full-time on the service. My own simple signal is how many people in my group at the temple get jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you drop the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If hiring in São Paulo stopped altogether, I'd go full-time on the service. I'd watch how many people in my group at the temple get jobs. That's my own simple signal.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to build a solid career and a **small business**.
Families and community groups should help those who fall behind.
think: I'm fairly hopeful: a job next year gives me four years to grow into a role that's **hard to replace**.
If not, the bakery service gives me income.

feel: Hopeful and busy, because I have a plan and a **backup**.
S3.quote: My own simple signal is how many people in my group at the temple get jobs.
fieldNote: Five years gives her a plan with a job, a side business and shared family savings.

steps.text: Take a job at a company that uses AI deeply
Keep the bakery app and its clients running
Save a third of every pay cheque
Join my parents in a small shared property fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good span, enough to build skills and a family. I'd say people should work, save and stay close to their communities, and that the market will make new jobs as it always has. I'd tell friends to be bold but not reckless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel good. I could be running my own software company by then, and the bakery might have three branches with my app inside. There will be new things to fix, and people to look after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job for three or four years to learn, then start my own company, with the bakery service as the first product. I'd save for a small flat, keep studying and support my parents and grandmother. I'd stay active in the temple group, where I find most of my friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and happy. Ten years feels like a real chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the first thing you'd build once you had your own company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tool for small food shops to plan stock, staff and prices, using what I learn at the bakery. I'd pay my first employees fairly, and I'd hire from my neighbourhood. If I'm lucky I'd hire my cousin who's good at sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A recession, or a platform changing the rules overnight. I'd keep a cash reserve, like my grandmother always told us. And I'd keep my feet on the floor of the bakery, which reminds me who I'm building for.

say: I'd say ten years is a good span, and the market will make **new jobs** as it always has.
I'd tell friends to be bold but not reckless.
think: I feel good: I could be running my own **software company**, and the bakery might have three branches.
There will be new things to fix and people to look after.

feel: Calm and happy, because ten years feels like a **real chance**.
S4.quote: I'd keep my feet on the floor of the bakery, which reminds me who I'm building for.
fieldNote: Calm follows from her adaptability, her working product and her family backing.
Her plans include hiring from the **neighbourhood** and paying fairly, a traditional community value.
She names her grandmother's advice about cash reserves as her risk plan.

steps.text: Work three or four years at a software firm to learn
Start my own company with the bakery service

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time to build anything solid. What would help is quick access to small loans for new businesses, fast retraining, and families and community groups that look after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'm afraid of using these tools every day. A little, because they may take work from people like me. But I'd rather be the person who knows how they work than the one who gets surprised. In my family we learn the hard way, and we don't quit.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be the person who knows how they work than the one who gets surprised.
portrait: Yara is a **computer engineering** graduate in São Paulo, living above her family's bakery, with 45 applications and no offer.
She uses AI tools every day and has built an ordering app that saves the bakery hours every week.
Her traditional values show in her trust of **family and community** over handouts.
Her mood runs from uneasy at most scenarios to anxious at two years, and calm at ten.
Her main plan is a service for small food shops, with a job on the side for learning.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI case, because there'd be no time to build anything solid.
whatWouldHelp: Quick access to **small loans** for new businesses and fast retraining.
Families and community groups that look after each other.
